Article Title: Elephant trapped in slush at Gunderipallam dam near Erode; rescue operations under way
Article Text:
Photo by S Parthiban





ERODE: A female elephant got trapped in slush at the Gunderipallam dam near Gobichettipalayam in Erode district, prompting a major rescue operation by forest and fire service personnel on Sunday.Wild animals have been frequently entering the dam vicinity in search of drinking water due to acute water scarcity in the forest. The water level in the Gunderipallam dam, located in the T N Palayam forest range, has dropped in recent weeks. In the early hours of Sunday, a female elephant that came to the dam to drink water got stuck in the slush in the exposed portion of the reservoir. “Unable to free itself, the animal struggled for several hours and was trumpeting in distress,” said a forest officer from the T N Palayam forest range.On being alerted by residents, officials and staff from the T N Palayam forest range and personnel from fire and rescue services rushed to the spot and launched rescue efforts.As the elephant had become exhausted after being trapped in the slush for several hours, teams began efforts to pull it out using ropes and an earthmover. However, the rescue operation suffered a setback when an earthmover deployed for the task got stuck in the muddy terrain.The incident delayed rescue operations.Forest authorities made alternative arrangements by bringing in another earthmover to rescue the elephant. A veterinary team from Sathyamangalam has been mobilised to provide medical assistance and monitor the elephant’s condition.
Article Summary: Wild animals have been frequently entering the dam vicinity in search of drinking water due to acute water scarcity in the forest. The water level in the Gunderipallam dam, located in the T N Palayam forest range, has dropped in recent weeks.

Article Title: Convict on parole flees to Andaman, CCTV helps nab him
Article Text: Madurai: A life convict from Tamil Nadu who absconded during parole flew to Andaman Islands , hoping to evade police and start a new life. But CCTV recording from a police station provided the crucial lead for Ramanathapuram police to unravel his escape plan, arrest him within days and return him to prison last week. Arun Pandian , 33, was serving life sentence at Madurai Central Prison when he secured 21 days’ parole last month for his mother’s eye surgery. He switched off his mobile phone and disappeared. When he failed to return to prison on Oct 2, police began searching but found no trace of him in Madurai, where his mother was undergoing treatment.The first breakthrough came when investigators reviewed CCTV footage from a local police station where Arun was required to report and sign during his parole under a court order. They noticed a man accompanying him during his visits. “Further investigation identified him as Arun’s friend Vinoth Kumar ,” said Antony Raj, sub-inspector at Kenikarai police station in Ramanathapuram.Police then traced Vinoth’s mobile phone records, which revealed his journey from Madurai to Chennai and subsequently to Port Blair in the Andaman Islands. Vinoth had returned to Ramanathapuram, where police tracked him down. During questioning, he disclosed that Arun had sought his assistance, borrowed his phone and planned the escape to Andaman with his help.Ramanathapuram ASP K Nehaa subsequently contacted her IPS training batchmates E Kathiravan and Abhijeet Sirohi, who helped obtain passenger details of those arriving in Andaman after Oct 2.Investigators used the information to narrow down Arun’s whereabouts.Nehaa said Arun was staying at a friend’s house and had secured employment at a local bar for Rs 15,000. She said Antony Raj and his team travelled to Andaman and, with local police assistance, located and arrested Arun last week. He was subsequently brought to Ramanathapuram.Arun had been sentenced to life imprisonment in 2021 for murdering his sister’s father-in-law following a family dispute in 2017.
Article Summary: Arun Pandian, 33, was serving life sentence at Madurai Central Prison. He secured 21 days’ parole last month for his mother’s eye surgery. When he failed to return to prison on Oct 2, police began searching but found no trace of him. CCTV footage from a police station provided the crucial lead.

Article Title: Two private buses fined for skipping Pallipalayam bus stand
Article Text: NAMAKKAL: Police imposed a fine of Rs 10,000 each on two private buses for failing to stop at the Pallipalayam bus stand in Namakkal district and causing inconvenience to passengers.A 3.5km flyover connecting Pallipalayam and Tiruchengode is widely used by commuters travelling to and fro Namakkal, Rasipuram and Erode. However, residents have complained that several govt and private buses frequently bypassed the Pallipalayam bus stand by using the flyover, leaving passengers stranded for long periods.Acting on the complaints, a police team led by Pallipalayam DSP Gauthaman conducted a vehicle inspection on the new flyover. The team intercepted two private buses that had bypassed the Pallipalayam bus stand without picking up passengers. “We counselled the drivers, pointing out that commuters were forced to wait for buses in heavy rain while operators continued to ignore them,” the DSP said.Police seized a high-decibel horn from one of the buses and imposed fines on two-wheeler riders for not wearing helmets and on motorists for violating one-way traffic rules.
Article Summary: Police impose fine of Rs 10,000 each on two private buses for failing to stop at bus stand. A 3.5km flyover connecting Pallipalayam and Tiruchengode is widely used by commuters travelling to and fro Namakkal, Rasipuram and Erode. Residents have complained that several govt and private buses frequently bypassed the bus stand by using the flyover.

Article Title: Land brokers arrested for murder of elderly woman in Salem
Article Text: SALEM: The Salem city police arrested two land brokers on Tuesday in connection with the murder of an elderly woman and the theft of her gold jewellery.N Janabai, 74, of Muniyappan Samy Koil Street in Kitchipalayam, was found strangled to death at her residence on Monday night. The murder came to light when her son, Sathish Kumar alias Senthil Kumar, 50, returned home after work. He found that her gold jewellery, weighing seven sovereigns, was missing.The Kitchipalayam police registered a case.Salem city police commissioner Joshi Nirmal Kumar formed a special team to investigate the case. Inquiries revealed that land broker A Sampath Kumar, 55, of Masinaickenpatti and S Vairamani, 70, of Kitchipalayam in the city murdered the woman and stole her seven sovereigns of gold jewellery. Later, the duo pledged the jewellery at a pawn shop. “The stolen ornaments have since been recovered,” said a police officer.Police found that Janabai had sold a portion of her land a few months ago and had been frequently approached by land brokers regarding the sale of her remaining properties. Sampath Kumar and Vairamani were among those who had allegedly visited her in connection with land transactions.Further investigations are under way.
Article Summary: N Janabai, 74, of Muniyappan Samy Koil Street in Kitchipalayam, was found strangled to death at her residence on Monday night. Her son, Sathish Kumar alias Senthil Kumar, 50, found that her gold jewellery, weighing seven sovereigns, was missing. The stolen ornaments have since been recovered.

Article Title: Sabarimala gold heist: Kerala HC directs authorities to expedite prosecution sanction process
Article Text:
Sabarimala Ayyappa temple

Kochi:





The high court on Monday directed the authorities to expedite the process of obtaining prosecution sanction in the Sabarimala gold theft case after being informed that the final report could not be filed because the appointed assistant legal adviser had not yet assumed charge.A bench of Justices V Raja Vijayaraghavan and K V Jayakumar issued the directive after SIT head S Sasidharan informed the court that, despite completing the investigation into one of the two cases — involving the alleged misappropriation of gold from the side frames of the sreekovil — the final report could not be filed before the jurisdictional court without prosecution sanction for offences under the Prevention of Corruption Act.He further submitted that the factual report and draft chargesheet had been prepared, and the assistant legal adviser in the vigilance department, whose assistance was required to complete the process, had been appointed and posted but had not yet assumed charge. Consequently, the requisite legal advice could not be incorporated into the proforma.Meanwhile, director general of prosecution T Asaf Ali assured the court that all necessary steps would be taken to ensure that the assistant legal adviser assumed charge and the requisite legal advice was obtained and incorporated into the proforma, enabling the matter to be placed before the competent authority for consideration of the prosecution sanction request.Accordingly, the court directed the authorities concerned to expedite the process, ensure that the requisite legal advice was obtained without delay, and place the prosecution sanction request before the competent authority. The SIT was also directed to ensure that the final report was submitted before the jurisdictional court without delay once sanction was obtained. The bench also directed the SIT to complete the investigation into the second case, involving the alleged misappropriation of gold from the coverings of the dwarapalaka idols, before Nov 25 and adjourned the matter to Nov 10.
Article Summary: The high court on Monday directed the authorities to expedite the process of obtaining prosecution sanction in the Sabarimala gold theft case. A bench of Justices V Raja Vijayaraghavan and K V Jayakumar issued the directive after SIT head S Sasidharan informed the court that the final report could not be filed without prosecution sanction.

Article Text:
Saka continues supporting underprivileged children through Big Shoe, providing access to healthcare, opportunities and brighter futures.

A recognition outside of football

Nigeria: 120 children

Restoring a child’s vision

A wide-ranging mission

A different type of win

Football’s biggest moments are often measured by goals, trophies and memorable nites under stadium lights. But for Bukayo Saka, one of the most meaningful victories has come away from the pitch, in hospitals, classrooms and communities where access to basic medical care can transform a child’s future. The Arsenal star’s continued humanitarian efforts have now earned him one of football’s biggest off-pitch honors. Scroll down to find out the details of his humanitarian act.Saka was named the winner of the 2026 Socrates Award at the Ballon d’Or ceremony in London, an award given to footballers whose humanitarian contributions extend beyond the sport, according to a report by The Cable. The prize, named in honor of the legendary Brazilian footballer, was first given in 2022 to former Liverpool forward Sadio Mane and has since become a major recognition of the role football plays in supporting social causes.The Standard reports Saka was recognized for his extensive humanitarian work with his family and several charitable organizations, particularly his long-standing involvement with Big Shoe, which provides medical assistance and humanitarian support to children and families in need around the world. The award was presented by Nigerian musician Burna Boy at the gala, held at the Palladium Theater in London, adds The Cable.Saka has worked with Big Shoe on initiatives to support children who may have trouble accessing necessary medical procedures, according to The Standard. In 2022, the Arsenal winger partnered with the charity to finance life-changing surgeries for 120 children in Kano, Nigeria, in one of the most significant efforts of his charitable work to date.His support went beyond Nigeria the following year. Saka also helped fund surgeries for another 100 children across Rwanda, Kenya and Tanzania, as part of broader efforts to bring critical healthcare to children in developing communities, The Cable reported. The work has a personal resonance with the cause. Saka, who is of Nigerian heritage, has long used his platform to support initiatives for children in worlds of situations from his own.Among the stories featured around Saka’s Socrates Award was that of 14-year-old Biringiro from Rwanda, whose eyesight was restored thanks to Big Shoe’s medical program. Biringiro had started losing his sight at the age of 12, The Standard reports. Living in a village without electricity, his failing eyesight had made it increasingly difficult to move around each day and had impacted his ability to fully participate at school.Thanks to treatment supported by Big Shoe, the young boy was able to regain his sight and go back to activities that had become difficult, including reading the classroom blackboard. His story was a powerful testament to the impact behind Saka’s charitable work, turning the award from a personal achievement into recognition of the children and communities benefitting from the initiative.Saka’s humanitarian efforts go beyond individual medical procedures. The footballer has been working with Big Shoe and his family to help children who do not have the same chances or resources as many others.The initiative also reflects the broader purpose of the Socrates Award: to highlight the ability of prominent athletes to use their visibility and influence to create meaningful change away from competition.Saka has emphasized the importance of helping children rediscover simple joys and possibilities that illness or poverty can take away, as The Standard reported. For young beneficiaries of Big Shoe’s work, that can mean something as fundamental as being able to see clearly, return to school or imagine a future without a medical condition that defines their possibilities.The 2026 Socrates Award adds another layer to Saka’s growing legacy. His footballing legacy with Arsenal may continue to define him, but his charitable work is creating an impact measured in lives, not in scorelines.Images Courtesy: Facebook and istock
Article Summary: Bukayo Saka was named the winner of the 2026 Socrates Award at the Ballon d'Or ceremony in London. The award is given to footballers whose humanitarian contributions extend beyond the sport. Saka has long supported Big Shoe, which provides medical assistance and humanitarian support to children and families in need around the world. In 2022, the Arsenal winger partnered with the charity to finance life-changing surgeries for 120 children in Nigeria.

Article Title: Five years after Rangers manager Walter Smith died, his widow Ethel chose the cancer unit that treated him to receive £50,000 from a charity, one of the biggest donations in the Scottish hospital's hi
Article Text:
Cancer unit that cared for Walter Smith

A charity established after a personal loss

Walter Smith's legacy beyond football

Five years after former Rangers and Scotland manager Walter Smith died following a battle with cancer, his widow Ethel has chosen to honour his memory by directing a £50,000 charitable donation to the hospital unit that cared for him. The gift, made through the Emmie Smillie Foundation, was presented to the cancer unit at Vale of Leven Hospital in Alexandria, Scotland, on October 26, 2026, the fifth anniversary of his death.According to STV News, Ethel nominated the unit in recognition of the treatment and support her husband received there. The donation is among the largest the hospital has received and will be used to improve facilities and make treatment more comfortable for patients. Hospital officials said the exact plans for spending the money were still being determined when the gift was announced.“When I was asked where I would like the money to go, I had no hesitation in nominating the unit here at the Vale,” Ethel said, explaining that the family wanted to acknowledge the care provided by the hospital. “Walter received treatment here, so it felt fitting as a thank you for the care we received from the unit and the hospital in general,” she added.The donation was formally presented to June Raines, the unit's charge nurse, and Gerry O'Hare, a former clinical nurse specialist who cared for Smith during his treatment. The contribution will support the unit's work serving patients from across the surrounding region.Vale of Leven Hospital is located in Alexandria, West Dunbartonshire, and provides cancer treatment and other services to patients in the west of Scotland. Its haematology-oncology unit offers day-care treatment, allowing many patients to receive care close to home without requiring an overnight hospital stay. According to Scottish News, the unit has 12 treatment chairs and a phlebotomy service. Its treatments and support include chemotherapy, blood transfusions and symptom management for people with cancer and blood disorders.For the Smith family, the hospital's importance went beyond its medical services. Ethel's decision to nominate the unit reflected the personal experience of receiving care during a difficult period. Gerry O'Hare, who now works part-time at the Beatson in Glasgow, said the donation would help support a service that had meant a great deal to Smith and his family.“Having worked at the Vale and knowing personally how much the unit meant to Walter and his family, it is wonderful to see such a significant donation coming back to support its patients,” O'Hare said, according to STV News. He added that the service was important to the local community and welcomed the foundation's contribution towards its continued work.June Raines also thanked the foundation, noting that the unit's ability to provide treatment locally helped patients avoid travelling farther for care. She said the funding would allow the hospital to enhance its facilities and improve the experience of people coming in for treatment.The donation was made through the Emmie Smillie Foundation, established by businessman Andy Smillie after his daughter died from cancer. The foundation raises money to support cancer services across Scotland through charitable contributions and fundraising activities.The latest gift is not the first time the organisation has supported Vale of Leven Hospital. STV News reported that the foundation had made a similar £50,000 donation to the hospital around four years earlier.The new contribution brings together two families' experiences of cancer and loss. The foundation was established in memory of Smillie's daughter, while Ethel's nomination reflects the care her husband received during his illness.The funding will be used to improve the hospital unit's facilities and patient experience, although the precise projects to be supported have not yet been announced. The hospital's leadership welcomed the donation, saying it would help staff continue providing compassionate care to patients and their families.Rebecca Reid, interim director for NHS Greater Glasgow and Clyde's Clyde Sector, thanked the foundation and Ethel for selecting the hospital. She said the money would help the unit improve the experience of patients receiving treatment at Vale of Leven.Smith died aged 73 on October 26, 2021, following a battle with cancer. He remains one of the most respected figures in Scottish football, particularly for his achievements with Rangers, where he enjoyed two successful spells as manager. During his first spell at Ibrox, Smith won 13 major trophies in seven years before becoming Scotland manager in December 2004. He returned to Rangers in 2007 and added another eight trophies before retiring in 2011 after completing a domestic double.He also managed Everton and led Scotland's national team for three years. His achievements made him a defining figure in Rangers' modern history, while his influence extended to players and fellow managers who worked with him.The donation arrives as supporters and the club continue to remember Smith five years after his death. However, its significance lies not only in the football manager's legacy but also in the practical support it will provide to people receiving cancer treatment.By nominating the unit that cared for her husband, Ethel has ensured that the family's gratitude will translate into support for other patients facing similar challenges. The £50,000 contribution will help the hospital improve its facilities and treatment environment, allowing Smith's memory to be associated with care for the community as well as his achievements on the pitch.
Article Summary: Walter Smith died aged 73 on October 26, 2011, following a battle with cancer. His widow Ethel nominated Vale of Leven Hospital in Scotland to receive a £50,000 donation. The donation was made through the Emmie Smillie Foundation. The money will be used to improve facilities and make treatment more comfortable for patients.

Article Title: In 1985, Dionne Warwick, Elton John, Gladys Knight and Stevie Wonder recorded a charity hit; the song helped raise millions for AIDS research as the epidemic was unfolding
Article Text:
How four music legends came together

Why the song mattered during the AIDS epidemic

How much money did the charity hit raise?

The song's success continued at the Grammys

A musical legacy beyond the charts

In 1985, as the AIDS epidemic spread and fear and misinformation surrounded the disease, four of the biggest names in music came together to record a song that would become a landmark charity hit. Dionne Warwick, Elton John, Gladys Knight and Stevie Wonder joined forces on That's What Friends Are For, turning a song about friendship and support into a fundraising effort for AIDS research. Released under the name Dionne & Friends, the single became a major commercial success, eventually raising millions of dollars for the American Foundation for AIDS Research, known as amfAR. It also earned major Grammy recognition, giving the campaign a reach far beyond the recording studio.The song was written by Burt Bacharach and Carole Bayer Sager and had originally been recorded by Rod Stewart for the 1982 film Night Shift. When Warwick took up the song for the charity project, the idea developed into a collaboration featuring Elton John, Gladys Knight and Stevie Wonder.The performers brought together distinct musical styles, creating a recording whose message of loyalty and solidarity resonated with listeners.The project was supported by Bacharach, Bayer Sager and record executive Clive Davis, with proceeds directed towards AIDS research. The single was released in 1985, at a time when public understanding of HIV/AIDS remained limited and the need for research funding was urgent.In the early 1980s, AIDS had become a growing public-health crisis, but the disease was still widely misunderstood. The first recognised cases in the US were reported in 1981. Researchers were working to understand the virus, develop diagnostic tools and identify effective treatments, while people affected by the epidemic often faced discrimination and social isolation.A significant scientific milestone came in March 1985, when the US Food and Drug Administration approved the first commercial blood test to detect HIV. The test helped identify infections and made it possible to screen donated blood more effectively. However, effective long-term treatment remained unavailable, and the epidemic continued to claim lives.Against this backdrop, a charity recording featuring four internationally recognised performers helped bring AIDS research to a much wider audience. Its impact extended beyond its message: the commercial success of the single generated substantial funds for research and helped keep the cause in the public eye.The recording raised approximately $3.4 million for AIDS research, according to the Recording Academy's retrospective on Bacharach's career. Other accounts describe the total more generally as more than $3 million. The money supported amfAR, an organisation established in 1985 that became a prominent funder of AIDS research and an advocate for people affected by HIV/AIDS.The fundraising achievement was especially significant because the song reached audiences who might not otherwise have engaged directly with the issue. Its success demonstrated how the music industry could use a commercially popular release to generate money and attention for a public-health cause.That's What Friends Are For became a major hit in the US, reaching No. 1 on the Billboard Hot 100 in 1986. It went on to win two awards at the 1987 Grammy Awards: Song of the Year, awarded to songwriters Bacharach and Bayer Sager, and Best Pop Performance by a Duo or Group with Vocal, awarded to Warwick, John, Knight and Wonder.The awards cemented the recording's place in popular music history. But its legacy was not limited to chart positions or industry recognition. The song became closely associated with a moment when artists used their collective influence to support AIDS research at a time of immense uncertainty.The significance of That's What Friends Are For lies in the combination of its message, its star-studded collaboration and its fundraising impact. The recording did not solve the AIDS crisis or directly produce a medical breakthrough, but it helped finance research and raise awareness when both were urgently needed.Decades later, the song remains a prominent example of how popular music can support a charitable cause. Its message of friendship took on a broader meaning during the epidemic, offering a reminder of the importance of solidarity with people affected by a disease that was still poorly understood.
Article Summary: Dionne Warwick, Elton John, Gladys Knight and Stevie Wonder recorded That's What Friends Are For in 1985. The single became a major commercial success, eventually raising millions of dollars for the American Foundation for AIDS Research. It also earned major Grammy recognition, giving the campaign a reach far beyond the recording studio.
